Newborn Care

Newborn Rash Guide: What Is Normal and When to Worry

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Most newborn rashes are harmless, show up in the first days or weeks of life, and clear on their own without any treatment. Blotchy red spots, tiny white bumps, pimples, flaky patches, and prickly heat bumps are all common on brand new skin. This guide walks through what each one looks like, how long it usually lasts, and how to tell a normal rash from one that needs a clinician the same day.

Erythema toxicum: the blotchy red rash most babies get

Erythema toxicum is the most common newborn rash, and its name is far scarier than the rash itself. It affects roughly half of full term newborns and usually appears in the first few days of life. You will see blotchy red patches, often with a small firm yellow or white bump in the center, scattered across the chest, back, face, arms, or legs. The spots can fade in one place and pop up in another within hours, which surprises many parents. Despite the dramatic look, your baby is not bothered by it. It is not an infection, not an allergy, and not a sign of anything you did wrong.

No treatment helps, and none is needed. The rash typically fades on its own within about two weeks, often sooner. Skip creams, ointments, and extra baths; they will not speed things up and can irritate new skin. The one caution is that a few serious conditions can look similar. Erythema toxicum spots have a blotchy red base with a tiny firm center, and the baby feeds and behaves normally. If the bumps look like true blisters or are filled with pus, if the rash appears alongside a fever, or if your baby seems unusually sleepy or unwell, have a clinician look the same day rather than waiting it out.

White bumps and baby acne: milia and newborn breakouts

Milia are the tiny white bumps many parents notice on a newborn's nose, chin, or cheeks in the first days. Each one is a small plug of skin protein trapped just under the surface, about the size of a pinhead, and they often come in clusters. They are not pimples, they are not contagious, and they do not hurt. Baby acne looks different: it shows up later, usually around two to four weeks of age, as red pimples and small bumps on the cheeks, forehead, and sometimes the chest. It can flare when your baby is warm or crying, and it often looks worst just before it starts to clear.

The care plan for both is the same: leave them alone. Milia clear on their own within a few weeks to a couple of months as the trapped protein works its way out. Baby acne usually fades within weeks as well, though it can linger a little longer in some babies. Do not squeeze, scrub, or pick, and skip acne washes and adult skin products entirely; they are far too harsh for newborn skin. Washing the face once a day with warm water and patting it dry is plenty. If a breakout is spreading, oozing, crusting, or still going strong after a few months, ask your baby's clinician to take a look.

Peeling, flaky skin in the first weeks

Peeling skin is normal in newborns and is usually a sign of a healthy transition, not dryness gone wrong. Your baby spent months in fluid, protected by a creamy coating called vernix. Once that coating wears off, the outer layer of skin flakes away, most visibly on the hands, feet, and ankles. Babies born at or after their due date often peel the most, because they had less vernix left at birth. The peeling typically starts in the first day or two and settles within one to three weeks on its own, revealing the softer skin underneath.

Less is more with newborn skin care, which matches the advice pediatric groups give. You do not need to peel the flakes off, and scrubbing only irritates the new skin below. Short baths a few times a week with plain warm water, or a mild fragrance free cleanser if you use anything, are enough. If the skin looks tight or cracked, a thin layer of a plain fragrance free moisturizer or petroleum jelly is fine. Deep cracks that bleed, skin that is red, weepy, and itchy, or peeling that comes with blisters is different from normal flaking and deserves a clinician's opinion.

Cradle cap and heat rash

Cradle cap shows up as yellowish, greasy scales or crusty patches on the scalp, and sometimes on the eyebrows or behind the ears. It usually appears in the first weeks to months, does not itch or bother your baby, and is not caused by poor washing. Gentle care is enough: wash the scalp with a mild baby shampoo, loosen soft scales with a soft brush or your fingertips, and let the rest lift over time. A small amount of baby oil, mineral oil, or petroleum jelly applied shortly before washing can soften thick patches. Most cradle cap clears within a few months, though it can come and go for a while before it is gone.

Heat rash looks like clusters of tiny red or clear bumps, usually in places that trap warmth: the neck folds, chest, upper back, and skin creases, or wherever clothing holds sweat against the skin. Newborn sweat glands are still immature, so babies overheat easily under too many layers or in a warm car seat. The fix is cooling, not cream. Move your baby somewhere cooler, remove a layer, and let the skin air dry. The bumps usually fade within a few days once the skin stays cool. A good rule for dressing is one more layer than feels comfortable for you, not several.

When a newborn rash needs a clinician

Most rashes on this list need nothing but time, so save your energy for the few signs that matter. Contact your baby's clinician right away if a rash comes with fever; any fever of 100.4 F (38 C) or higher in a baby under three months needs medical attention the same day, not a wait and see approach. Also call the same day for blisters, pus filled spots, rapidly spreading redness that is warm or tender, or a baby who is unusually sleepy, floppy, or feeding poorly. Go to emergency care immediately for small purple or dark red spots that do not fade when you press the skin, since a rash that does not blanch can be a sign of serious infection.

For everything milder, a photo and a note beat a worried memory. Rashes change fast, so take a picture in good light and jot down when it started, where it spread, and anything new like a formula change or a detergent switch; the BeMama app is a handy place to keep those notes for your next visit. Two look alikes belong to other conversations: yellowing skin is jaundice rather than a rash, and redness or oozing around the cord stump has its own care steps. When you are unsure, calling is always reasonable. Clinicians expect newborn rash questions, and no one will fault you for asking.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Newborn skin, nails, diaper care, and umbilical healing usually need gentle handling, clean water, fragrance-free products when needed, and keeping the cord area clean and dry. Normal appearance changes should still be discussed when caregivers are uncertain.

Spreading redness, swelling, pus, foul odour, persistent bleeding, fever, blisters, or a baby who seems unwell can signal a problem that needs professional assessment.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to save dated skin or cord observations and questions for visits. Photos and notes do not diagnose infection or determine whether a product is safe.

When to seek help

Contact a clinician promptly for signs of infection, fever, poor feeding, or a rapidly worsening rash. Use emergency care for severe illness or breathing difficulty.

Sources and further reading

  • American Academy of Pediatrics — Fever and Your Baby
  • Public Health Agency of Canada — Make Your Home Safe for Your Child

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Most newborn rashes, including erythema toxicum, milia, and baby acne, clear on their own without treatment.
  • Peeling skin in the first one to three weeks is a normal transition, not a problem to fix.
  • Less is more: plain warm water, fragrance free products, and no scrubbing or squeezing.
  • Heat rash means your baby is too warm, so cool the skin instead of reaching for creams.
  • Call a clinician for fever with a rash, blisters or pus, fast spreading redness, or a baby who seems unwell.

Frequently asked questions

When should I worry about a newborn rash?

Worry when a rash comes with fever, blisters, pus filled spots, rapidly spreading redness, or a baby who is unusually sleepy or feeding poorly. Any fever of 100.4 F (38 C) or higher in a baby under three months needs medical attention the same day. Purple or dark red spots that do not fade when pressed need emergency care immediately. Everything else on this page can usually wait for a routine call or visit.

What does baby acne look like?

Baby acne looks like small red pimples and bumps on the cheeks, forehead, and sometimes the chest, usually starting around two to four weeks of age. It can look worse when your baby is warm or crying. It clears on its own within weeks to a few months, and acne products or scrubbing should never be used on newborn skin.

Is newborn skin peeling normal?

Yes, peeling skin is normal in the first one to three weeks, especially on the hands, feet, and ankles. Babies born at or after their due date often peel the most. Plain warm water and, if the skin looks tight, a fragrance free moisturizer are enough; see a clinician if the skin cracks deeply, bleeds, or looks red and weepy.

What is erythema toxicum in newborns?

Erythema toxicum is a harmless and very common newborn rash of blotchy red patches, often with a small yellow or white bump in the center, that appears in the first days of life. It affects roughly half of full term newborns, needs no treatment, and typically fades within about two weeks. Have a clinician check the same day if spots look like blisters, fill with pus, or come with a fever.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
